He called me Malala

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.....we meet Malala, the Pakistani girl who survuved being shot by the Tabliban and Nobel Peace Laureate

Summary:
"He Named Me Malala" is an upcoming American documentary film directed by Davis Guggenheim. The film is about a young Pakistani female activist Malala Yousafzai, who was targeted by Taliban gunmen, shot in the head and left wounded. Guggenheim is an Oscar winner and the film tells the story of Malala and her remarkable family. A pre-release junket has been organized by Fox Searchlight pictures and Carte Blanche had the opportunity to attend the junket and have one-on-one interviews with her, Guggenheim and her father.

Further information:
Plot Summary:
"He Named Me Malala" is an intimate portrait of Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Malala Yousafzai, who was targeted by the Taliban and severely wounded by a gunshot when returning home on her school bus in Pakistan’s Swat Valley. The then 15-year-old (she turns 18 this July) was singled out, along with her father, for advocating for girls’ education, and the attack on her sparked an outcry from supporters around the world. She miraculously survived and is now a leading campaigner for girls’ education globally as co-founder of the Malala Fund.

Acclaimed documentary filmmaker Davis Guggenheim ("An Inconvenient Truth," "Waiting for Superman") shows us how Malala, her father Zia and her family are committed to fighting for education for all girls worldwide. The film gives us an inside glimpse into this extraordinary young girl’s life – from her close relationship with her father who inspired her love for education, to her impassioned speeches at the UN, to her everyday life with her parents and brothers.

“One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world." – Malala

Malala's story:
Malala Yousafzai born 12 July 1997) is a Pakistani activist for female education and the youngest-ever Nobel Prize laureate. She is known mainly for human rights advocacy for education and for women in her native Swat Valley in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of northwest Pakistan, where the local Taliban had at times banned girls from attending school. Yousafzai's advocacy has since grown into an international movement.

Her family runs a chain of schools in the region. In early 2009, when she was 11–12, Yousafzai wrote a blog under a pseudonym for the BBC detailing her life under Taliban occupation, their attempts to take control of the valley, and her views on promoting education for girls in the Swat Valley. The following summer, journalist Adam B. Ellick made a New York Times documentary[3] about her life as the Pakistani military intervened in the region. Yousafzai rose in prominence, giving interviews in print and on television, and she was nominated for the International Children's Peace Prize by South African activist Desmond Tutu.

On the afternoon of 9 October 2012, Yousafzai boarded her school bus in the northwest Pakistani district of Swat. A gunman asked for her by name, then pointed a pistol at her and fired three shots. One bullet hit the left side of Yousafzai's forehead, travelled under her skin through the length of her face, and then went into her shoulder. In the days immediately following the attack, she remained unconscious and in critical condition, but later her condition improved enough for her to be sent to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham, England, for intensive rehabilitation. On 12 October, a group of 50 Islamic clerics in Pakistan issued a fatwā against those who tried to kill her, but the Taliban reiterated their intent to kill Yousafzai and her father, Ziauddin Yousafzai.

The assassination attempt sparked a national and international outpouring of support for Yousafzai. Deutsche Welle wrote in January 2013 that Yousafzai may have become "the most famous teenager in the world." United Nations Special Envoy for Global Education Gordon Brown launched a UN petition in Yousafzai's name, demanding that all children worldwide be in school by the end of 2015; it helped lead to the ratification of Pakistan's first Right to Education Bill.

A 2013 issue of Time magazine featured Yousafzai as one of "The 100 Most Influential People in the World". She was the winner of Pakistan's first National Youth Peace Prize, and the recipient of the 2013 Sakharov Prize. In July that year, she spoke at the headquarters of the United Nations to call for worldwide access to education, and in October the Government of Canada announced its intention that its parliament confer Honorary Canadian citizenship upon Yousafzai. Even though she is fighting for women's and children's rights, she did not describe herself as feminist when asked on Forbes Under 30 Summit. In February 2014, she was nominated for the World Children's Prize in Sweden. In May, Yousafzai was granted an honorary doctorate by the University of King's College in Halifax. Later in 2014, Yousafzai was announced as the co-recipient of the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle against the suppression of children and young people and for the right of all children to education. Aged 17 at the time, Yousafzai became the youngest-ever Nobel Prize laureate

Press Release:


She's known worldwide as the Pakistani girl who, three years ago as a 15-yer-old, defied the Taliban and demanded that girls be allowed to receive an education. Her stance soon saw her shot in the head by a Taliban gunman, but she survived to become the youngest ever Nobel Peace Prize Laureate at 17 years old. Carte Blanche meets Malala Yousafzai in London for an exclusive interview, ahead of the release of a new documentary film on her extraordinary life.

Script:


Malala:
Education went from being a right to being a crime. Girls were stopped from going to school. I had two options. One was to remain silent and wait to be killed. And the second was to speak up and then be killed.
LINK:
She decided to speak up and for that she got shot in the face at point blank range. Her name is Malala Yousafzai, the youngest ever recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize.
V/O:
She grew up in Pakistan’s Swat Valley, an area of breath-taking natural beauty. It was also a peaceful part of the country – until the Taliban showed up.

V/O:
The Swat Valley has, like the rest of Pakistan, come under attack from the Taliban who want to create a Muslim State based on strict Sharia or Islamic Law. And they are ruthless in eradicating all those who oppose their plans.

LINK:
In October 2012 the Taliban focused their efforts on a single person. A formidable opponent whom they considered a massive threat to their ideals. An opponent they just had to eliminate. This opponent was a 15 year old girl.
V/O:
It was Malala. This Taliban leader, Maulana Fazlullah, issued an order to assassinate her. On 9 October 2012, while aboard this school vehicle she was shot on the right side of her face. The bullet travelled down into her neck and lodged in her shoulder. In a critical condition she was rushed to hospital. Her life hung by a thread and doctors gave her very little chance of survival.

She was a thorn in the side of the Taliban for one simple reason – she openly advocated for education for girls in Pakistan. Under the Taliban, this was forbidden. Malala dared to publically criticise this. This, the Taliban could not tolerate.
Ziauddin:
The Taliban wanted to snag that voice. They wanted to silence her forever. She is becoming a voice for the people of Pakistan, a voice for peace, a voice for education, a voice for many girls in Pakistan. That’s why they wanted to make her silent forever.
V/O:
Ziauddin Yousafzai – Malala’s father - accompanied her when she was first rushed to hospital and later transferred to the UK for specialized treatment.
LINK:
This incident attracted global attention and propelled Malala and her quest against the Taliban onto the world stage. Little by little her remarkable story began to emerge.
V/O:
Malala’s father was passionate about education and had founded a chain of schools the Swat Valley. He had long been one of the few Pakistani advocates for equal rights for women and girls, so when his eldest daughter was born he named her “Malala” after a legendary Pashtun heroine who once inspired her people to fight for freedom and was killed as a result.
Ziauddin:
What happened in our life, I never imagined about it. But when I named her it was just that this girl will have all freedom, independence, she will have a voice, education. She will play a full-fledged role in life like any man in the community. The basic thought was that she would be an independent powerful person.
V/O:
And Malala lived up to her name. When she was only 11 she started to speak out against the Taliban closing schools. She criticised them openly on radio, and later she also wrote a regular blog for the BBC. In Pakistan she became well-known as the advocate for girls’ education.

The Taliban's attempt to kill Malala received worldwide condemnation and led to protests across Pakistan. What happened to her forced the world to focus on the plight of the 66 million girls worldwide being denied a formal education.
LINK:
Malala slowly recovered from her wounds and the family relocated to the UK, and became a global spokesperson for children’s education, especially education of girls.
V/O:
Next week a documentary film about her life will be released in South Africa. Carte Blanche had the opportunity to interview Malala in London ahead of the release of the film. She believes that the Taliban made a tactical error by attacking her.
Malala:
I think they have made a mistake because they targeted a person who was not going to get afraid or to get scared or to stop her journey. When I was attacked, after that I feel stronger than before because now I have realised that no one can stop me. Even that is supporting me in my cause and that wants me to continue, God wants me to continue and speak on behalf of children.
V/O:
The new documentary film is one way for Malala to continue to speak on behalf of children the world over.

And for director of the film, Davis Guggenheim and Malala’s father, the project was about far more than making just another film.
Ziauddin:
This is our dream and this is our destiny and this is Davis’s dream. He always says that this is not a movie, it is a movement. So, we will be happy if it brings goodness to this world.
V/O:
Although he has directed a number of blockbuster documentaries such as “An Inconvenient Truth”, the making of this film was a once-in-a-lifetime experience for Davis.
Davis:
Not many people know the family that I have met. This beautiful family that has fun, that laughs, wrestles, argues and it has this real dimension. For me that was a revelation that these are not these untouchable heroes. They’re courageous people but they are also real people. I wanted people to fall in love with Ziauddin and Malala the way I have.
LINK:
In the film one gets a glimpse of the other members of the family, Malala’s mother and two younger brothers as they adjust to their new life in England.
UPSOUND
……….it is a first impression.
Davis:
What’s beautiful about this movie and the reason why I think people in SA will love it, it is really a movie about a family. About a father and a daughter. A father who inspires and a daughter that is courageous.
V/O:
A year after her ordeal at the hands of the Taliban, this courageous daughter addressed the United Nations on her birthday.
UPSOUND:

Gordon Brown:
Let me say the words the Taliban never wanted her to hear: “Happy 16th birthday, Malala”

Malala:
“It is an honour for me to speak again after a long time……. And my dreams are the same’
V/O:
The 2013, 14 and 15 issues of Time magazine featured her as one of "The 100 Most Influential People in the World".

Malala has become a household name, won numerous awards, and has had an honorary doctorate bestowed on her by the University of King's College in Halifax.
Malala UPSOUND: “Thank you”
V/O:
Malala and her family are Muslim, but she distances herself from the brand of Islam the Taliban propagates.
Malala:
What the Taliban or other terrorist groups are doing it is totally their own interests. For me that is not Islam. My Islam is peace, its humanity, it is justice, it is equality. And I am a Muslim and I am fighting for education and I am fighting for peace. That is my Islam. It is love, it is peace. (Eerste deel 00:06:52 – 00:07:12)
LINK:
Last year in December, at the tender age of only 17, Malala become the youngest Nobel Peace Prize Laureate
Malala:
At the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony I mentioned that I’m not a lone voice, I’m many. I am the voice of all children who are deprived of education.
V/O:
At the ceremony Malala thanked her father.
Malala:
Thank you to my father for not clipping my wings and letting me fly.
V/O:
Malala’s story continues to inspire and she has shared her dream with many world leaders. But despite her fame and high profile, she considers herself an average teenager.
Malala:
I think I am just a normal person. It is not that I am totally perfect. I do fight with my brothers and my parents do get angry with me and tell me to stop fighting with them and I do have to do my homework and I do have to go to school.
V/O:
And she has a teenager’s crush on a tennis player.
Malala:
Roger Federer
Shots van Roger Federer
Malala:
Laughs
V/O:
She manages to balance her private life with a very busy public one.
Malala:
There is so much to do. School, homework and other things. But I try to divide it equally and when it comes to school, I say no to everything. For example, if its speeches or campaigning -- all during holiday time. School time, no, just homework and schoolwork.
LINK:
Malala gaan volgende jaar studeer.
V/O:
However, this extraordinary young girl never loses sight of her purpose.
Malala:
At night when I sleep I think that when I continue this mission, I will be able to one day see every child go to school which is my dream and my ultimate goal.
V/O:
For the past 2 years Malala’s family life has been documented for the making of the film.
Malala:
This camera captured almost all those moments which I always wanted to remember. My time in Jordan with Syrian refugee children or my time in Nigeria or Kenia. I’m hopeful that this movie will be able to spread across the world to say that I wasn’t only one girl that was stopped from going to school or who has gone through terrorism but there are millions across the world.
V/O:
Davis shares this dream with Malala.
Davis:
For me, just making a movie and telling a beautiful story is not enough. The challenge now is to make this a movement, it’s not just a movie. And we know that when you educate a girl, you not only transform her life, you transform her family, her village, and you transform her nation. We must get the message out all around the world.
V/O:
The message that must go out is very simple.
Malala:
One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world.

A father who inspires and a daughter that is courageous. V/O: A year after her ordeal at the hands of the Taliban, this courageous daughter addressed the United Nations on her birthday. UPSOUND: Gordon Brown: Let me say the words the Taliban never wanted her to hear: “Happy 16th birthday, Malala” Malala: “It is an honour for me to speak again after a long time……. Malala UPSOUND: “Thank you” V/O: Malala and her family are Muslim, but she distances herself from the brand of Islam the Taliban propagates. metadata.Summary: "He Named Me Malala" is an upcoming American documentary film directed by Davis Guggenheim. The film is about a young Pakistani female activist Malala Yousafzai, who was targeted by Taliban gunmen, shot in the head and left wounded. Guggenheim is an Oscar winner and the film tells the story of Malala and her remarkable family. A pre-release junket has been organized by Fox Searchlight pictures and Carte Blanche had the opportunity to attend the junket and have one-on-one interviews with her, Guggenheim and her father.
metadata.Further information: Plot Summary: "He Named Me Malala" is an intimate portrait of Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Malala Yousafzai, who was targeted by the Taliban and severely wounded by a gunshot when returning home on her school bus in Pakistan’s Swat Valley. The then 15-year-old (she turns 18 this July) was singled out, along with her father, for advocating for girls’ education, and the attack on her sparked an outcry from supporters around the world. She miraculously survived and is now a leading campaigner for girls’ education globally as co-founder of the Malala Fund. Acclaimed documentary filmmaker Davis Guggenheim ("An Inconvenient Truth," "Waiting for Superman") shows us how Malala, her father Zia and her family are committed to fighting for education for all girls worldwide. The film gives us an inside glimpse into this extraordinary young girl’s life – from her close relationship with her father who inspired her love for education, to her impassioned speeches at the UN, to her everyday life with her parents and brothers. “One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world." – Malala Malala's story: Malala Yousafzai born 12 July 1997) is a Pakistani activist for female education and the youngest-ever Nobel Prize laureate. She is known mainly for human rights advocacy for education and for women in her native Swat Valley in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of northwest Pakistan, where the local Taliban had at times banned girls from attending school. Yousafzai's advocacy has since grown into an international movement. Her family runs a chain of schools in the region. In early 2009, when she was 11–12, Yousafzai wrote a blog under a pseudonym for the BBC detailing her life under Taliban occupation, their attempts to take control of the valley, and her views on promoting education for girls in the Swat Valley. The following summer, journalist Adam B. Ellick made a New York Times documentary[3] about her life as the Pakistani military intervened in the region. Yousafzai rose in prominence, giving interviews in print and on television, and she was nominated for the International Children's Peace Prize by South African activist Desmond Tutu. On the afternoon of 9 October 2012, Yousafzai boarded her school bus in the northwest Pakistani district of Swat. A gunman asked for her by name, then pointed a pistol at her and fired three shots. One bullet hit the left side of Yousafzai's forehead, travelled under her skin through the length of her face, and then went into her shoulder. In the days immediately following the attack, she remained unconscious and in critical condition, but later her condition improved enough for her to be sent to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham, England, for intensive rehabilitation. On 12 October, a group of 50 Islamic clerics in Pakistan issued a fatwā against those who tried to kill her, but the Taliban reiterated their intent to kill Yousafzai and her father, Ziauddin Yousafzai. The assassination attempt sparked a national and international outpouring of support for Yousafzai. Deutsche Welle wrote in January 2013 that Yousafzai may have become "the most famous teenager in the world." United Nations Special Envoy for Global Education Gordon Brown launched a UN petition in Yousafzai's name, demanding that all children worldwide be in school by the end of 2015; it helped lead to the ratification of Pakistan's first Right to Education Bill. A 2013 issue of Time magazine featured Yousafzai as one of "The 100 Most Influential People in the World". She was the winner of Pakistan's first National Youth Peace Prize, and the recipient of the 2013 Sakharov Prize. In July that year, she spoke at the headquarters of the United Nations to call for worldwide access to education, and in October the Government of Canada announced its intention that its parliament confer Honorary Canadian citizenship upon Yousafzai. Even though she is fighting for women's and children's rights, she did not describe herself as feminist when asked on Forbes Under 30 Summit. In February 2014, she was nominated for the World Children's Prize in Sweden. In May, Yousafzai was granted an honorary doctorate by the University of King's College in Halifax. Later in 2014, Yousafzai was announced as the co-recipient of the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle against the suppression of children and young people and for the right of all children to education. Aged 17 at the time, Yousafzai became the youngest-ever Nobel Prize laureate
